title: Rows and rounds
subtitle: Flat versus tubular fabric, and what each means for your stitch pattern
excerpt: Working in rows builds flat fabric — you turn at the end of each row and work back. Working in rounds builds tubular or circular fabric — you never turn. The two are not interchangeable: a stitch pattern designed for rows will look different worked in rounds.
sourceNotes: Pauline Turner, How to Crochet — rows and rounds construction. Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886).

glossaryTerms.definition: The face of the fabric intended to be seen. In flat row work the right and wrong sides alternate as you turn. In round work the right side always faces outward.
The back of the fabric, not intended to be seen in the finished piece. Working rows means the wrong side faces you on alternate rows.

content.text: Working in rows means crocheting to the end of a row, turning the work 180 degrees, and working back in the opposite direction. The
faces you on odd rows and faces away on even rows. Working in rounds means crocheting continuously in one direction — the right side always faces outward and the
is always on the inside of the tube or circle.
Flat pieces: dishcloths, scarves, garment panels, blanket squares worked flat.
Pieces shaped by increasing/decreasing row width: triangular shawls, graded increases on a yoke.
Pieces that will be seamed: traditional garment fronts and backs worked separately then joined.
Tubes: seamless sleeves, hat bodies, socks, bag bodies.
Circles and ovals: basket bases, amigurumi bodies, flat medallion motifs.
Seamless garments: top-down yoke constructions where body and sleeves are all round.
Why rows and rounds give different results

In rows you work alternately from left-to-right and right-to-left. In rounds you work only in one direction (usually right-to-left for right-handers). For plain stitches this makes no visual difference. But for stitch patterns that look asymmetric — most textured patterns, post stitches, colour-work floats — the direction changes the result. A pattern written for rows will not look the same worked in rounds unless the author has adjusted it.

Rows need a turning chain at the start of each new row to bring the yarn up to the stitch height. Rounds replace this with a starting chain at the beginning of each round. The height rules are identical: ch1 for double crochet, ch2 for half treble, ch3 for treble, ch4 for double treble. Whether the starting chain counts as a stitch depends on the pattern — always check.
